easy.heading: Starting My Morning With Some Simple Sums
easy.body:
I sat down with my first cup of coffee and dove into the easy puzzle. It felt like a gentle way to wake up my brain. The first thing I noticed were the sum constraints at the top corners. Since (0,0) and (0,5) both needed to be 6, I knew I had to use my dominoes with sixes right away. I placed the [6,0] domino at (0,0) and (1,0) and then the [4,6] domino at (0,5) and (1,5). It felt like the puzzle was already halfway done!

Next, I looked at the middle. There was an empty spot at (2,1) which meant nothing could go there. That forced my [3,1] domino into a vertical position. The sum of 2 at (2,2) was a big clue because it meant that cell had to be a 2. Looking at my remaining pieces, the [2,3] domino was the only one that fit. Once I placed the 2 at (2,2), the 3 ended up at (2,3). Since (2,3) and (2,4) had to be equal, I knew (2,4) also had to be a 3. It all clicked into place after that.

medium.heading: Tackling The Triple Equals Challenge
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today was a bit of a step up, mostly because of those equals regions that spanned three different cells. I immediately looked at the region covering (1,2), (1,3), and (1,4). They all had to have the same value. I scanned my domino list and realized I had a [2,2] and a [1,1], which are always great for these kinds of spots. I also noticed two empty squares at (0,3) and (4,1). These act like walls that help you figure out where your dominoes can and cannot lie.

The real breakthrough happened when I looked at the bottom. The region at (3,2) and (3,3) had to be less than 2, which is a very tight limit. That meant those cells could only be 0 or 1. At the same time, the cell at (2,2) had to be greater than 4, which usually means a 5 or 6. By balancing these high and low requirements, I was able to slot the [5,2] and [4,2] dominoes in a way that satisfied those tricky greater than and less than signs. It took a minute of shuffling, but once the middle row was set, the rest followed naturally.

hard.heading: Navigating The Sea Of Zeros
hard.body:
The hard puzzle today from Rodolfo Kurchan was a real test of patience. The first thing that jumps out is the sheer number of zero sums. When you see a target of 0, you know exactly what pip value goes there, but the challenge is figuring out which domino provides it. I spent a lot of time staring at the cluster of zeros in the middle of the grid at (2,3), (2,4), and (2,5). Since these were all zeros, I had to carefully pick which dominoes from the set, like [0,4] or [0,2], could reach those spots without breaking the surrounding sums.

I hit a bit of a dead end near the bottom right. There are several empty cells like (3,4), (3,6), and (4,4) that really restrict your movement. I realized that the dominoes with higher values, like [4,4] and [3,4], had to go in the few spots that weren't zero-heavy. The turning point was realizing that the sum of 4 at (4,2) had to be paired with a zero at (3,2) because of the domino [4,0]. Once I committed to that vertical placement, the whole bottom row started to make sense. It was like a giant game of logic Tetris!

explanation.tips: Try to look for the most restrictive rules first, like cells that must be zero or empty squares that act as barriers. If you get stuck, look at your list of dominoes and see which ones are unique, like doubles or those with high numbers, as they can only fit in a few specific regions. Always remember that an empty cell is just as important as a numbered one because it limits how you can orient your dominoes.
explanation.learned:
Today really taught me the power of the equals constraint. In the medium puzzle, seeing three cells in a row that had to be identical narrowed down the domino choices much faster than the sum constraints did. It makes you look for patterns in the domino set rather than just doing mental math.

I also realized that in the harder puzzles, the zeros are actually your friends. They might seem boring, but they provide a solid anchor point that you can build the rest of your solution around. It is a good reminder to start with what you know for sure and work outward from there.

faqs.question: How do you play the NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Pips is a logic puzzle where you place a set of dominoes into a grid. Each cell in the grid has a rule, like a sum, an equality, or a comparison, that must be satisfied by the number of pips on the domino half placed in that cell.

faqs.question: What does an empty cell mean in Pips?
faqs.answer: An empty cell in a Pips puzzle means that no domino can be placed in that specific square. It acts as a permanent gap in the grid that helps you determine the orientation of nearby dominoes.

faqs.question: Are there always the same dominoes in every Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: No, the set of dominoes changes based on the size of the grid and the difficulty level. You can see the list of available dominoes for each puzzle to help you track which ones you have already used.

faqs.question: What is the best strategy for solving hard Pips puzzles?
faqs.answer: The best strategy is to look for the most constrained cells first, such as those with a sum of 0 or a very high target. Use the empty cells to block off impossible placements and keep track of your available dominoes to see which ones are forced into certain spots.

faqs.question: Who creates the NYT Pips puzzles?
faqs.answer: Pips puzzles are often edited by Ian Livengood and feature designs from various puzzle constructors like Rodolfo Kurchan, who created today's challenging hard mode grid.
